source_text: Εἰ τοίνυν τὴν περὶ τὸ ἐπιστύφειν τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα οἰκονομίαν, ἀγαθὴν οὖσαν καὶ σωτήριον, ἀναγκαίως ὑπὸ τοῦ λόγου παραλαμβανομένην ἐπεδείξαμεν πρός τε μετάνοιαν καὶ πρὸς τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τὴν κώλυσιν εὔθετον γενομένην, ἑξῆς ἂν εἴη σκοπεῖν τὸ ἤπιον τοῦ λόγου· δίκαιος γὰρ οὗτος ἀποδέδεικται καὶ τὰς ἰδίας παρατίθεται γνώμας τὰς πρὸς σωτηρίαν παρακλητικάς, δι᾿ ὧν καὶ τὸ καλὸν καὶ τὸ συμφέρον πατρικῷ θελήματι γνωρίζειν ἡμῖν βούλεται. σκόπει δὲ ταῦτα· τὸ μὲν καλὸν τοῦ ἐγκωμιαστικοῦ, τὸ δὲ συμφέρον τοῦ συμβουλευτικοῦ· καὶ γὰρ οὖν τοῦ μὲν συμβουλευτικοῦ σχέσις τὸ προτρεπτικὸν καὶ ἀποτρεπτικόν, τοῦ δὲ ἐγκωμιαστικοῦ τὸ ἐπαινετικόν τε καὶ ψεκτικὸν γίνεται. πῶς γὰρ ἔχουσα ἡ διάνοια ἡ συμβουλευτικὴ προτρεπτικὴ γίνεται καὶ πῶς ἔχουσα ἀποτρεπτική. ὡσαύτως δὲ καὶ τὸ ἐγκωμιαστικὸν πῶς μὲν ἔχον ψεκτικὸν γίνεται, πῶς δὲ ἔχον ἐπαινετικόν· περὶ ἃ καταγίνεται μάλιστα ὁ παιδαγωγὸς ὁ δίκαιος ὁ τοῦ ἡμετέρου συμφέροντος ἐστοχασμένος. ἀλλὰ γὰρ τὸ μὲν ψεκτικὸν καὶ ἀποτρεπτικὸν εἶδος ὑποδέδεικται ἡμῖν ἤδη πρότερον, νῦν δὲ αὖ τὸ προτρεπτικὸν καὶ ἐπαινετικὸν μεταχειριστέον καὶ καθάπερ ἐπὶ ζυγοῦ τὰς ἰσοστασίους ἀντισηκώσωμεν τοῦ δικαίου πλάστιγγας. Τῇ μὲν οὖν ἐπὶ τὰ συμφέροντα προτροπῇ ὁ παιδαγωγὸς διὰ Σολομῶντος ὧδέ πως χρῆται· »ἐγὼ ὑμᾶς, ἄνθρωποι, παρακαλῶ καὶ προΐεμαι ἐμὴν φωνὴν υἱοῖς ἀνθρώπων· ἐπακούσατέ μου, σεμνὰ γὰρ ἐρῶ« καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. συμβουλεύει δὲ τὰ σωτήρια, ὅτι ἡ συμβουλὴ πρὸς αἵρεσίν ἐστι καὶ φυγὴν ἐπιτήδειος, καθάπερ ποιεῖ διὰ τοῦ Δαβὶδ λέγων »μακάριος ἀνὴρ ὃς οὐκ ἐπορεύθη ἐν βουλῇ ἀσεβῶν καὶ ἐν ὁδῷ ἁμαρτωλῶν οὐκ ἔστη καὶ ἐπὶ καθέδραν λοιμῶν οὐκ ἐκάθισεν· ἀλλ᾿ ἢ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ κυρίου τὸ θέλημα αὐτοῦ.« τῆς δὲ συμβουλίας μέρη τρία, τὸ μὲν ἐκ τῶν παρεληλυθότων χρόνων λαμβάνον τὰ παραδείγματα, οἷον τί ἔπαθον οἱ Ἑβραῖοι τῷ χρυσῷ εἰδωλολατρήσαντες ἐν μόσχῳ, καὶ τί ἔπαθον ἐκπορνεύσαντες καὶ τὰ ὅμοια, τὸ δὲ ἐκ τῶν παρόντων χρόνων κατανοούμενον, οἷον αἰσθητικῶς καταλαμβανόμενον, ὡς ἐκεῖνο εἴρηται πρὸς τοὺς ἐρομένους τὸν κύριον »εἰ αὐτὸς εἶ ὁ Χριστός, ἢ ἄλλον περιμένομεν«· »ἀπέλθετε. καὶ εἴπατε Ἰωάννῃ· τυφλοὶ ἀναβλέπουσιν, κωφοὶ ἀκούουσιν, λεπροὶ καθαρίζονται, ἀνίστανται νεκροί, καὶ μακάριός ἐστιν ὃς ἐὰν μὴ σκανδαλισθῇ ἐν ἐμοί.« τοῦτ᾿ ἄρα ἦν ὃ προφητεύων εἴρηκεν Δαβὶδ »καθὼς ἠκούσαμεν, οὕτως καὶ εἴδομεν«. ἐκ δὲ τῶν μελλόντων τὸ τρίτον συνίσταται μέρος τῆς συμβουλίας, ᾧ τὰ ἀποβησόμενα κελεύει φυλάττεσθαι· καθὸ κἀκεῖνο εἴρηται· »οἱ δὲ ἁμαρτίαις περιπεσόντες βληθήσονται εἰς τὸ σκότος τὸ ἐξώτερον· ἐκεῖ ἔσται ὁ κλαυθμὸς καὶ ὁ βρυγμὸς τῶν ὀδόντων« καὶ τὰ παραπλήσια· ὡς ἐκ τούτων εἶναι συμφανὲς διὰ πάσης θεραπείας χωροῦντα τὸν κύριον εἰς σωτηρίαν ἐκκαλεῖσθαι τὴν ἀνθρωπότητα. τῇ δὲ παραμυθίᾳ παρηγορεῖ τὰ ἁμαρτήματα, μειῶν μὲν τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν, ἅμα δὲ καὶ ἐλπίδα ἐνδιδοὺς εἰς σωτηρίαν.
thought_title: The Gentle Guidance of the Lord
pass_a_gloss: If therefore we have shown that the economy concerning the conversion of humanity, being good and salvific, is necessarily received from the Word for repentance and for the prevention of sins, it would be next to consider the gentleness of the Word; for this Word has been shown to be just and sets forth its own counsels, which are persuasive towards salvation, through which it wants us to know what is good and profitable by the paternal will. Consider these things: the good is of the encomiastic, the profitable is of the advisory; for the advisory has a relationship that is both protreptic and apotreptic, and the encomiastic becomes both praiseworthy and blameworthy. For how does the mind that has advisory become protreptic and how does it become apotreptic? Similarly, the encomiastic, how does it become blameworthy and how does it become praiseworthy? The righteous Pedagogue, who has considered our profit, is concerned with these things. But since the blameworthy and apotreptic type has already been shown to us before, now we must use the protreptic and praiseworthy, and as if on a balance, let us weigh the equal weights of the righteous scales. The Pedagogue, therefore, uses the protreptic towards what is profitable through Solomon, saying: 'I, men, exhort you and extend my voice to the sons of men; hear me, for I will speak dignified things' and the following. He advises the salvific things, because the advice is for choosing and fleeing, as he does through David, saying: 'Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly and has not stood in the way of sinners and has not sat in the seat of the pestilential.' The parts of the advice are three: one taking the examples from past times, such as what the Hebrews suffered when they idolized the golden calf, and what they suffered when they fornicated, and similar things; one considering the present times, such as what is perceived sensibly, as was said to those asking the Lord: 'if you are the Christ, or if we should wait for another'; 'go and tell John: the blind see, the deaf hear, the lepers are cleansed, the dead rise, and blessed is he who is not scandalized in me.' This, therefore, is what David prophesied, saying: 'as we have heard, so we have seen.' The third part of the advice is established from future things, which commands to guard against the things that will happen; as it is also said: 'but those who have fallen into sins will be cast into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth' and similar things. It is clear from these things that the Lord, through every therapy, calls humanity to salvation. With the consolation, he comforts the sins, lessening the desire, and at the same time giving hope for salvation.

pass_b_english: Since we have shown that the arrangement for converting humanity — an arrangement that is good and salvific — is necessarily received from the Word for repentance and for preventing sins, the next thing to consider is the Word's gentleness. The Word has been shown to be just, and he sets forth his own counsels, which are persuasive toward salvation; through these he wants us to know what is good and profitable by the Father's will (Proverbs 8:4-6). Consider these matters: the good belongs to the encomiastic mode, the profitable to the advisory mode. The advisory mode relates both to urging on and to turning away, while the encomiastic mode becomes both praising and blaming. How does the advisory mind become urging, and how does it become turning away? Likewise, how does the encomiastic become blaming, and how does it become praising? The righteous Paedagogus, who has aimed at our profit, is concerned with these very things. But the blaming and turning-away kind has already been shown to us earlier; now we must employ the urging and praising kind, and, as on a balance, weigh the equal weights of the just scales.

The Paedagogus therefore uses the urging toward what is profitable through Solomon, saying: "I call to you, O men, and I lift my voice to the children of men. Hear me, for I will speak noble things" (Proverbs 8:4-6) and what follows. He advises the things that save, because advice serves for choosing and fleeing, just as he does through David: "Blessed is the man who does not walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in the law of the Lord" (Psalm 1:1-3). Advice has three parts: one takes its examples from past times — for instance, what the Hebrews suffered when they worshipped the golden calf, and what they suffered when they committed fornication, and similar things; a second is understood from present times — that is, what is perceived by the senses, as was said to those asking the Lord, "Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?" — "Go and tell John: the blind receive their sight, the deaf hear, the lepers are cleansed, the dead are raised, and blessed is the one who is not offended by me" (Matthew 11:4-6). This, then, is what David prophesied: "As we have heard, so have we seen." The third part of advice is constituted from future things, which commands us to guard against what will happen; as it is also said: "Those who fall into sins will be thrown into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth" (Matthew 8:12) and similar passages. It is clear from these that the Lord, through every therapy, calls humanity to salvation. With consolation he comforts sins, lessening desire and at the same time giving hope for salvation.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex rhetorical terminology (encomiastic, advisory, protreptic, apotreptic) and the tripartite structure of advice. Scripture citations in Pass B are correctly identified and added to the text (Proverbs 8:4-6, Psalm 1:1-3, Matthew 11:4-6, Matthew 8:12) to match the Greek allusions/quotes. Pass A serves as a faithful literal bridge.
